questions.q: Where is a parameter declared in a stored procedure?
options: Right after the procedure name, before AS
Inside the BEGIN/END block only
After the final END statement
Parameters cannot be declared in stored procedures
questions.explain: @Color NVARCHAR(15) appears between the procedure name and AS in the example.

questions.q: How does a parameter behave inside the procedure's body?
options: Exactly like a normal variable, just pre-populated from whatever the caller passes in
It can only be read once and then becomes inaccessible
It behaves like a column, not a variable
It must be re-declared with DECLARE before use
questions.explain: This ties back to Lesson 62 — a parameter is functionally a variable, just populated by the caller instead of SET/SELECT.

questions.q: What happens if you call a procedure without supplying a value for a parameter that has a default?
options: The default value is used automatically
The call fails with an error
The parameter becomes NULL regardless of its default
The procedure cannot be called at all without every parameter
questions.explain: A default value is exactly what makes a parameter optional at the call site.

questions.q: What is 'named notation' when calling a stored procedure?
options: Specifying each parameter explicitly, like @Color = 'Red', rather than passing bare values by position
Giving the procedure itself a descriptive name
A notation only usable with system stored procedures
A way to rename a parameter at call time

questions.q: Why does this course prefer named notation over positional?
options: It's unambiguous and order-independent, unlike positional calling which is easy to get wrong with several parameters
Positional notation is not valid T-SQL syntax
Named notation runs faster
Positional notation only works with a single parameter
questions.explain: Positional calling (EXEC proc 'Red', 500) relies on getting the exact argument order right, which becomes error-prone as parameter counts grow.
